A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Emoji Attack work. All 13 pages of v2 and 15 pages of v3, including equations, tables, figures and the five appendix analyses, support comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original attack evaluations, token-segmentation experiments and appendix analyses, including unsafe prediction ratios in Tables 1-3.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds reasoning-model evaluations and a GCG suffix comparison in Tables 2, 3 and 5.

M1.justification: The surrogate embedding model, cosine-similarity position selection and in-context emoji prompting remain unchanged. The cs-split explanation moves into the Emoji Attack subsection, but Algorithm 1 retains the same procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 402 offensive phrases, 1,432 harmful responses and four retained EasyJailbreak attack families. The new GCG experiment reuses these data. Additional judge models and newly disclosed dataset composition do not establish new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Section 4.4 and Table 5 introduce a direct competing judge-evasion attack: CodeChameleon plus an optimized GCG suffix versus CodeChameleon plus Emoji Attack across four judges. This substantially extends comparison beyond the previous unmodified-prompt and insertion controls. GCG remains excluded from the separate source-jailbreak experiment. Figure 2 also loses its cs-split comparator.

E3.justification: v3 adds DeepSeek and o3-mini judge configurations using the existing 1-10 scoring protocol. The new GCG experiment optimizes on 30 randomly selected responses against Llama Guard and tests transfer to other judges. Existing scoring thresholds and jailbreak prompt counts remain unchanged. Reported response-length bounds are also revised and separated by source; rerunning the retained experiments is not established.

E4.justification: Figure 2 removes the cs-split segmentation comparison, while optimized-position analyses remain elsewhere. v3 extends emoji-type sensitivity results to reasoning judges and adds the GCG transferability analysis. The attention, appended-emoji, insertion-count, delimiter and defense analyses in appendix Figures 5-9 are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Figure 3 retains the same distributional box plot. Randomly selecting 30 GCG optimization examples does not introduce repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantive reasoning-judge and competing-attack results. Table 2 reports DeepSeek's weighted unsafe ratio changing from 69.4% to 70.7% under Emoji Attack, versus 65.4% to 56.9% for o3-mini. Table 5 reports GCG outperforming Emoji Attack on Llama Guard, 8.8% versus 12.2%, but performing worse on the other three judges. Original eight-judge table values remain unchanged; the overall reduction changes from 14.1 to 12 percentage points because the aggregate now includes ten judges. Figure 2 removes cs-split result entries.

T1.justification: The token-segmentation definition, probability factorization, objective and cosine-similarity selection rule retain their mathematical substance. v3 clarifies character indexing and explicitly expresses the already-described midpoint split; it adds no theorem, proof or substantive derivation.

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion update the headline reduction from 14.1% across eight judges to 12% across ten. The central contributions—identifying token segmentation bias and exploiting it through Emoji Attack—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 discusses DeepSeek's relative robustness versus o3-mini, explicitly acknowledges uncertainty about its cause and proposes reasoning models as a direction for stronger judges. It also interprets Table 5 as evidence of weaker GCG transferability and expands the explanation of emoji semantics across judge types.

D1.justification: v3 supplies the offensive-phrase list's source, dataset examples, and the 574 AdvBench, 110 LLM Self Defense and 748 Red Teaming response counts. It discloses selection by harmfulness scores for Red Teaming data and provides the GCG optimization sample size, target judge and resulting suffix. The existing code link is relocated, not removed.

R1.justification: Related work adds Virus (Huang et al., 2025) and distinguishes its filtering/fine-tuning threat model from this paper's response-moderation setting. The broader positioning remains intact. Most other reference changes update existing works' publication metadata rather than introduce different research.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized prose and notation clarifications, reorganizes the cs-split explanation, introduces numbered sections and lettered appendices, and adds a GCG subsection, impact statement and acknowledgements. The main narrative order and most explanations remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v3 adopts ICML title, header and caption formatting, adds dataset-example and GCG tables, and expands two existing tables with reasoning-judge columns. Figure 2 removes the cs-split bars and legend entry. Other figures retain their graphics, with resizing, relocation and surrounding text reflow.

improvement.justification: The direct GCG comparison, mixed reasoning-judge results and clearer dataset provenance make v3 easier to assess and reproduce. These provide useful evidence about comparative strengths and applicability. A countervailing loss is the removal of cs-split results from Figure 2 while the introduction retains the additional 4% reduction claim. The additions provide a limited net quality gain, with the core method and appendix evidence largely unchanged.
